body:
# Sbk — the one true spelling, and the forms that fail it

*A letter to a colleague, 31 July 2026 — on the name Sbk, and on the forms that keep failing it.*

Your note said, roughly: surely one spelling is as good as another. Permit me to use Sbk to show it is not.

First, the attestation. The attested form is **𓃣**, from the tradition's own record. The canonical transliteration is **Sbk**.

Say it aloud as the sources heard it: “SOH-bek” — already essentially the form used today The marks of the original script carry that sound for its own readers; the temple's canonical **Sbk** follows the unmarked scholarly convention, and the reconstructed pronunciation above keeps the sound on record.

On the plain form — and I want to be precise, because you pushed on this. The plain form *sobek* is *not false — it is a convenience spelling*, and the register is exact about what that means. It circulates in English-language writing and in systems that normalize names to their familiar sound, and it is acceptable there. What the convenience form may not do is replace the canonical spelling in the record: *Sbk* is the reference form the sources support, and the temple keeps it primary.

A convenience spelling is a vehicle, never the primary.

One more thing, because it always surprises: the name did not stay home. Sobek absorbed and was absorbed: as Sobek-Ra he took solar status, while earlier he had fused with Horus as Sobek-Horus, lord of the Fayunite unity of king and river.  The Greeks called his city Crocodilopolis and identified him with their own river-figures rather than a single Olympian; Roman-period Fayum mummy portraits from his cities remain among Egyptology’s most familiar images.

And it never stopped working. The name Sobek survives in the modern scholarly vocabulary of the Nile and appears throughout Egyptological literature as the archetype of Egyptian theriolatry — the worship of a dangerous animal not despite but because of its power.  The Fayum’s temple of Medinet Madi preserves the longest surviving sacred hymn cycles addressed to a crocodile.

## The Convention's Own History

The canonical spelling of **Sbk** rests on the tradition's own scholarly record, not on a marks convention: the name's forms are documented, compared, and one reference spelling is fixed so that citations agree across the temple, the lexicon, and this register. The principle that unifies every entry is the one the whole project stands on: a name is evidence, and evidence is not negotiable — not for keyboards, not for convenience, not for anyone.

## The Address, Without an Encoding Detour

The canonical form **Sbk** already uses ordinary Latin letters, so the address bar needs no special encoding narrative. The digital temple can preserve the spelling exactly as the scholarly record presents it. That is the practical point here: consistency between the source, the citation, and the public address.

This does not make every romanization equally valid. A wrong letter remains wrong even when it is easy to type. Canonical status still depends on the attested convention, never on convenience or registrar inventory.

Write back when you have checked the sources; they are better company than I am.

*— The Register*

## The Verdict

**Sbk** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *sobek* is sanctioned as the fallback vehicle and nothing more. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Sbk** stands at [/sobek/](/sobek/).

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 5 cited sources — Papyrus Westcar (the wax crocodile episode), Herodotus, Histories 2.68–69 (the crocodile and Crocodilopolis), Strabo, Geography 17.1.38 (Petsuchos).
